name: Elizabeth I of England
summary: A Tudor monarch who defended royal authority and an established Protestant church governed by bishops, with herself as Supreme Governor. She resisted Parliament's attempts to dictate marriage, succession and religion, enforced conformity while avoiding systematic persecution, and pursued a mostly defensive but privateering foreign policy. Her writings say little on economics or social questions.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: She ruled as hereditary queen for 44 years and described herself as God's instrument and a monarch ruling with her subjects' love (Golden Speech, Tilbury).

parliament-supreme.rationale: She vetoed and forbade debate: in 1566 she ordered the Commons not to treat of the succession and told them she would 'never be by violence constrained'; on religion in 1585 she told Parliament she would handle clergy faults herself.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mixed: she used the prerogative (patents overriding statutes, gag orders), yet in 1601 said her grants must not oppress and that she must answer before a higher judge.

head-commands-forces.rationale: At Tilbury she declared she would be general of the army herself, appointing Leicester as lieutenant; she chose her own ministers and advisers (Cecil, Walsingham).

church-by-bishops.rationale: She upheld the episcopal church, told the bishops in 1585 to mend faults or be deposed, and rejected Puritan reformers; episcopacy stayed under the 1559 settlement.

national-church-status.rationale: The 1559 Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity set the Church of England as the established church with the Crown as Supreme Governor, and she defended it against Catholics and Puritans.

separate-church-state.rationale: She made herself Supreme Governor of the church, and told Parliament in 1585 that religion was her charge and she would depose negligent bishops.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Act of Supremacy placed ecclesiastical jurisdiction under the Crown, and she threatened bishops with deposition; no evidence read here on curbing church property.

clerical-rule.rationale: Authority over the church lay with the queen, who told bishops in 1585 that she would depose them and in 1585 refused clergy and Puritan claims to judge her government.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Act of Uniformity she secured imposed fines for absence from the established service and required the prayer book; the state enforced one public worship.

restrict-conversion.rationale: After the 1570 papal bull Parliament made converting subjects away from allegiance to her a treasonable offence (1581), though she mitigated other anti-Catholic bills; evidence of her own stance is partial.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: She described herself as raised high by God and ruling 'under God', as His instrument, while also stressing her subjects' love; no explicit statement denying popular source.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Mixed: in her January 1603 letter to James VI she says the Dutch were no longer bound to a ruler who broke his covenants and she backed their revolt against Philip II, but she treated resistance to her own rule as treason (Mary Stuart, Essex) and the 1585 remark against subjects judging their prince is not in saved texts.

death-penalty.rationale: She approved the trial of Mary Queen of Scots and gave direction for her execution for treason in 1587; the 1571 Treasons Act punished such crimes by death.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: For Mary Stuart she preferred a special commission over indictment and a jury under the 1585 act, saying strict common-law form would be absurd for one of her estate.

suppress-opposition.rationale: She suppressed Puritan nonconformity and conventicles and in 1566 forbade debate on the succession; she also took the Commons' petitions and answered them.

territorial-expansion.rationale: She granted Gilbert licence to take and hold lands not held by a Christian prince, backed the Raleigh enterprise, and the privateering war on Spain.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Her 1578 patent allowed settlers to occupy lands inhabited by 'heathen and barbarous' peoples so long as no Christian prince held them.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: By the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch she sent an army to support the Dutch rebels against Philip II.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Her forces put down the Irish revolts, including Desmond's rising in Munster, in part to deny Spain a base.

no-business-privileges.rationale: In 1601 she said grants harmful to her people should not stand under colour of patents, and issued a proclamation reforming patent abuses.

ban-cartels.rationale: She cancelled the worst monopoly patents in 1601 after complaints of price-fixing, though she had granted them and kept chartered monopolies like the East India Company.

leader-cult.rationale: Her image as Gloriana was deliberately promoted through portraits and pageants; she accepted public praise of her person.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The July 1596 open letter in her reign ordered 'Blackamoores' to be taken out of the realm, but it was largely ineffective and a 1601 draft was never issued; contested.

strong-leader.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

more-religion-public.rationale: 1585 speech closing Parliament (as quoted in Robertson, History of America): religion is the ground on which all other matters take root; says nothing of a larger public role, and she enforced uniformity.

right-to-secede.rationale: She defended Dutch resistance to broken covenants but rejected Irish separation.

population-transfer.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

religious-exemptions.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

elective-rulers.rationale: She retained her inherited crown and treated succession as a royal question.

non-intervention.rationale: In January 1603 she justifies intervening against Spanish government in the Netherlands.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: 1584 Raleigh patent: she reserves a fifth of all gold and silver ore and keeps new lands in English allegiance; one charter drafted formally, not a statement on how colonies are governed.

dynastic-succession.rationale: She held the crown by Tudor inheritance and told Parliament in 1563 and 1566 that succession was for the Prince to settle; she had no child and named no heir, so succession by a child is not tested.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Tilbury account endorses armed resistance to invasion, including personal participation.

spiritual-nature.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Chapter V, August 1595: her instructions authorize offensive attacks on Spanish fleets and possessions.

open-diplomacy.rationale: In her July 1602 letter she explicitly promises secrecy over alliance negotiations.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: 1577 letter to the bishops: she orders that all worship and preaching follow strictly the orders established by law and bans unlicensed exercises; a single church order took legal precedence.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: 1584 Raleigh patent authorises settling 'heathen and barbarous' lands not held by a Christian prince, with no condition for the people living there; a formal patent, not a stated view.

notes:
Her 1601 monopolies retreat is treated as her latest position on patents. Wording of the Collected Works was searched from a full-text scan. Not retrieved: Luminarium Golden Speech page, Fordham, Wikisource Act of Uniformity, text of the 1571 act and Poor Law 1601; the Poor Law and 1596 policy are ministerial/contested and so mostly unanswered. 'Windows into men's souls' comes only via Bacon, so is not counted.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass using original correspondence and archival transcripts. Routine acts merely assented to are excluded.
